references.text: Matthew's parallel to the parable of the sower: the seed sown on rocky ground receives the word with joy, but has no root in itself and falls away when trouble or persecution comes.
Mark's parallel to the parable of the sower: those sown on rocky ground receive the word with joy, but have no root and endure only for a short time.

Warning against an evil and unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God. Encouragement to hold fast to the beginning of our confidence until the end, paralleling the theme of temporary faith and falling away in Luke 8:13.
Describes those who have once been enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift but then fall away—a theme closely related to those who believe for a while and later fall away in time of testing.
Paul asks the Galatians: 'You ran well! Who hindered you from obeying the truth?'—illustrating the theme of a promising beginning that does not hold firm.
Describes those who have escaped the world's impurities by knowing the Lord, but are again entangled and overcome—paralleling temporary faith and falling away.

James encourages endurance in trials, since the testing of faith produces perseverance. This sheds light on the theme of standing firm in πειρασμός (trial) as opposed to falling away, as described in Luke 8:13.
The preceding verse in Luke's version of the parable, where some seed fell on rocky ground and withered because it had no moisture—the physical description interpreted in verse 13.
Paul urges the Colossians to remain firm in their faith, rooted and built up, not being shaken from the hope of the gospel—the opposite of lacking root and falling away.
Matthew's version of the parable itself: the seed that fell on rocky ground sprang up quickly but withered because it had no root—the basis for the interpretation concerning temporary faith.
